speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) how will the recent recycling requirements on large water users affect business costs; and (b) whether the Government will be providing any additional support to help affected businesses amidst rising costs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) whether there has been a change in the cost of producing NEWater and desalinated water since 2017; (b) what is the difference between the current marginal cost and long-run marginal cost of producing water in Singapore; and (c) whether the Government considers that there will be a need to increase water prices within the next five years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In Singapore, the water price is pegged to the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This includes the cost of building and upgrading water infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Pricing water on this basis allows the Public Utilities Board (PUB), Singapore's national water agency, to finance its long-term investments sustainably to meet future water demand and safeguard Singapore’s water security.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Operating expenses for chemicals needed for water production have grown by 33% due to global supply chain disruption and higher transportation cost.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Maintenance expenses have risen by 18% due to higher costs for contracted services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Construction costs have also gone up by 35%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Together, these cost pressures have led to an increase in PUB’s operating expenditure by around 30% since the last water price revision in 2017.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: PUB has undertaken various measures to moderate the impact of these cost drivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include leveraging energy-efficient technologies to reduce energy consumption, harnessing engineering solutions to offset higher construction costs and optimising and digitalising processes to reduce chemical and maintenance expenses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For example, at the new Tuas Water Reclamation Plant (TWRP), PUB avoided the construction of a long deep-sea outfall costing $650 million by adopting membrane bio-reactor technology to treat used water to an adequate standard for near-shore discharge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: TWRP will also generate 80% of the energy it requires for used water treatment, compared to only 25% for the conventional Ulu Pandan and Jurong WRPs it will replace, through enhanced primary treatment of used water and synergies from co-locating with the Integrated Waste Management Facility.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Despite such cost-saving measures, the cost of producing and supplying water, and collecting and treating our used water, remains significantly higher than the current water price.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Government will continue to review the water price regularly to ensure that water is right-priced.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As announced by the Ministry of Finance (MOF) last week, the Government will provide financial support to mitigate the impact of the water price increase and other cost of living concerns, especially for lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This includes additional U-Save rebates of $20 per quarter in 2024 and 2025 for all Singaporean HDB households.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The additional rebates will, on average, fully offset the increase in utility bills for 1- to 2-room HDB households and offset about 80% of the increase in utility bills for 3- to 4-room HDB households during this period.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With these rebates, 3- and 4-room households will see increases of only about $2 per month in their utility bills.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Besides right-pricing water to safeguard our water security, it is also important that we manage the growth in our water demand.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is especially so in the non-domestic sector, which will account for about two-thirds of our water demand by 2065.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about water recycling requirements for companies which are large water users and Government support for them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: From January next year, PUB will mandate minimum water efficiency requirements on new projects in water-intensive industries, with high potential for water recycling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: By recycling water, companies can recover the cost of their investments over time and enjoy cost savings in the longer term through reduced water usage.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Based on our estimates, the payback period for installing such recycling infrastructure ranges from two to four years for wafer fabrication companies and less than one year for the electronics and biomedical companies.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: PUB also works with businesses with high water consumption to identify ways to reduce consumption through their Water Efficiency Management Plans, or WEMP.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Everyone – individuals, households, community and businesses – has a part to play in conserving and using water wisely.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With right pricing and sustainable growth in water demand, we can continue to ensure a sustainable water system and safeguard water security for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Given that the subsidies are for new equipment, how can the Government further support businesses that have already invested in equipment and these equipment typically last 10 to 20 years, and also prevent these cost increases from being passed down to consumers?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Obviously, it varies from business to business and it will impact the more water-intensive industries more.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But in that sense, for the water-intensive users, companies that use more water, it is to their benefit and they are incentivised to look into water conservation projects and improve their water efficiency.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, we have upped our Water Efficiency Fund in order for them to implement such water recycling projects.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition to that, as the Member has said, there will probably be some existing infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Indeed, the Water Efficiency Fund is also available for innovative technologies to be implemented, for instance, in order to conserve or save water usage as well as, of course, to audit and identify where else there are opportunities for water savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First supplementary question: I agree with the Senior Minister of State that right pricing is important.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, is it possible to reduce the water price increase for households by introducing a progressive, multi-band pricing system to replace the current two-band system?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is fairer because, as the Senior Minister of State has said, most of the future increases in water consumption will come from the larger users in the non-household sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second supplementary question: can the Senior Minister of State confirm that the current water pricing formula has already taken into account fully the cost of producing water from our local sources?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, can Singaporeans expect that, barring unforeseen changes in ingredient costs, including energy, the water price will not shoot up drastically after the expiry of the Johor Water Supply Agreement in 2061?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to right pricing, first, I am happy to note that the Member said that he agrees with us that we need to right price water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But perhaps the Member's concept would differ from what we mean by "right pricing".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that will also take into account investments in additional facilities, additional water infrastructure, as well as renewing existing water infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As to the Member's question about tiered pricing – I think that is what the Member is saying – beyond the threshold of 40 cubic metres and above, as I have said, when we say "right price" water, we want to reflect the scarcity value of water, that water is precious from the very first drop.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, in order to do that and encourage consumers to save water and use water wisely, we need to price it properly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And that is the price of the next drop, the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, everybody, whether it is individuals, households, businesses and communities, ought to pay the right price for water and that is why we do not have additional bands.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Having said that, an average household uses about 15 cubic metres of water monthly.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For a four-person household, it is maybe about 18 cubic metres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have a higher tariff for those who use above 40 cubic metres.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The higher tariff is in place to encourage and incentivise households to use water wisely and conserve water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the Member's second question on whether the cost of producing water, say, from the local catchment has been fully priced, as I have said, the price of water is pegged to the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And to ensure water security, we have a blend of water, not just from local catchment, imported water, but also desalinated and NEWater.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: When I say the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water, as I have said, we also take into account long-term investments to meet future water demand and that will take into account the fact that water demand will increase and we will have to invest in additional capacities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister of State why such a short interregnum, as compared to the pre-2018 increase, before which prices are going up again for water?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is there any scope, policy space, for the Government to delay this increase with a view towards the profits generated by the authorities vis-a-vis water and the supply of water?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second question is with regard to the household water consumption patterns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand they have been on the down over the past few years, although it saw an uptick during the COVID-19 pandemic – and, understandably so, because most people were at home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With this as a backdrop, can I query the relevance of the water conservation tax as opposed to the Government's implementation of more water-efficient features for households, which is a more effective policy tool to encourage lower consumption of water and achieve the outcome that the Ministry is looking at with regard to ensuring that every Singaporean sees the first drop of water as a very scarce resource?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, is there space for the Government to reconsider the utility of its water conservation tax?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is it achieving the policy purpose that is intended?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or are water-efficient features actually a more likely source of realising water savings from household consumers?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to the first question about the earlier increase of 30% in 2017 and the current increase of 18%, as I have explained earlier in my reply, the latest revision in water price which would actually only take effect from 1 April 2024 and not now – is really due to external cost pressures.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And I have listed the increase in costs: due to electricity cost, which increased by 37%, and construction cost which increased by 35%.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The electricity cost increase is just from tariff increase.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Actual increases could be higher, depending on when we contracted our energy contracts and so on.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And then, there are maintenance cost increases due to increased manpower as well as chemical costs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, that is the reason why the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water has exceeded our current water price and there is a need to have a price revision in order to ensure that PUB can continue to sustainably cover its operating costs as well as continue to make investments in water infrastructure to ensure reliable water supply as well as water security.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But if we look at the revenue, the net income generated, whatever is generated, is actually ploughed back, reinvested, to fund the operating expenditure of the water system and, as I have said, in terms of ongoing investments, as well as additional investments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Some people talk about $2.4 billion and so on, of net surplus.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Between 2018 and 2022, it is $1.5 billion, but that is really needed, as I have said, to fund the operating expenditure as well as investments.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, the capital investments required then to meet future demand was $3 billion.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Therefore, PUB has had to, in addition, borrow from the market and issue bonds.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For instance, last year, in 2022, we issued $800 million in green bonds.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We borrowed from the market for long-term infrastructure projects.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, there is no profit; everything is actually reinvested or used.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With regard to whether it is better to use water efficiency features to incentivise water conservation efforts instead of the water conservation tax, first of all, the water conservation tax, is a tax, as the Member has rightly noted, to reflect the scarcity value as well as to incentivise consumers to use water wisely.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But the water tariff, together with the water conservation tax, is actually part of the price of water, which reflects the cost of producing and supplying the next drop of water.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: So, it is actually part of the water price.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Then, the waterborne tax is a tax contribution to the used water system.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Speaker, maybe I would just add, too – because I did not reply to water efficiency features – I would say that both are needed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And if we were to have further new demand, we are going to continue to tap on the more expensive sources of water, for example, desalination and recycled water.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Perhaps, some industries are consuming too much that does not make sense for us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And for some of the new investments, when we look at them, do they make sense for us, from a water resource standpoint?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, is the Government doing an exercise on that as well, to review the mix of our industry, whether it makes sense for us from a water resource standpoint?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: It may be because of the nature of the industry and the processes needed, like our wafer fabrication factories for instance, where water is needed.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: But it does not mean that they are not using water efficiently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Having said that, indeed, we continue to work with the industries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The mix of industries is something that the economic agencies, together with us, will have to continue to study.
